questions.sec: Language vs Speech & the Auditory Pathway
questions.q: The book defines language as which of the following?
opts: The basic concept of communication, a dominant-hemisphere function
questions.exp: Language is defined as the basic concept of communication and is a dominant-hemisphere function; its abnormality is aphasia. (Book p566)

questions.sec: Language vs Speech & the Auditory Pathway
questions.q: Speech, per the opening definition, is which, and its abnormality is which?
opts: Motor output of language, whose abnormality is dysarthria
questions.exp: Speech is the motor output of language; its abnormality is dysarthria, whereas the abnormality of language is aphasia. (Book p566)

questions.sec: Language vs Speech & the Auditory Pathway
questions.q: In the auditory-pathway diagram, prosody (emotional intonation of language) is attributed to which hemisphere?
opts: The dominant hemisphere at Broca's area
The dominant hemisphere at Wernicke's area
questions.exp: The diagram marks prosody - emotional intonation of language - as a non-dominant hemisphere function. (Book p566)

questions.sec: Language vs Speech & the Auditory Pathway
questions.q: A lesion severs the connecting fibres between the primary auditory area and Wernicke's area. Which deficit does the diagram label this as?
questions.exp: The auditory-pathway diagram labels connecting-fibre abnormality as pure word deafness; the peripheral muscles (larynx vocal cords, pharynx palate, oesophagus) are driven below the brainstem nuclei. (Book p566)

questions.sec: Language vs Speech & the Auditory Pathway
questions.q: Which pairing of the speech areas' functions is printed in the perisylvian diagram?
opts: Broca's (44,45): grammar, syntax, rhythm, fluency; Wernicke's (22): processing sound, comprehension
questions.exp: Broca's speech area (44,45) carries grammar, syntax, rhythm and fluency while Wernicke's area (22) processes sound and comprehension; the companion Areas-of-Brain diagram labels the perisylvian region, premotor, primary motor, supplementary motor, Rolandic fissure, primary sensory, supramarginal and arcuate gyri, Sylvian fissure and primary auditory area. (Book p566)

questions.sec: Language vs Speech & the Auditory Pathway
questions.q: Below the brainstem nuclei, the pathway diagram lists which peripheral effectors of speech?
opts: Tongue, soft palate and neck flexors only
questions.exp: The diagram's final line lists the peripheral muscles: larynx (vocal cords), pharynx (palate) and oesophagus. (Book p566)

questions.q: The note lines on this page pair which lesion with which deficit?
opts: Fusiform gyrus -> auditory agnosia; connecting fibres -> transcortical aphasia
Auditory association fibres -> auditory agnosia; connecting fibres -> pure word deafness; fusiform gyrus -> pure alexia
Auditory association fibres -> pure alexia; fusiform gyrus -> pure word deafness
Connecting fibres -> auditory agnosia; fusiform gyrus -> global aphasia
questions.exp: Notes: auditory association fibres abnormality -> auditory agnosia; connecting fibres abnormality -> pure word deafness; lesion in fusiform gyrus -> pure alexia. (Book p567)

questions.q: Per the lesion-site table, a lesion anterior to the central sulcus impairs which function?
questions.exp: Lesion/disease table: anterior to central sulcus -> fluency; posterior to central sulcus -> comprehension; in and around Sylvian fissure -> repetition; dominant lobe -> naming. Prosody of speech is d/t non-dominant lobe disease. (Book p567)

questions.q: In the aphasia flowchart, a patient has preserved comprehension and preserved repetition. Which aphasia is reached, and its stated cause?
opts: Conduction aphasia, d/t arcuate fasciculus lesion
Transcortical motor aphasia, d/t watershed infarct (MCA, PCA)
questions.exp: Preserved comprehension with preserved repetition leads to transcortical motor aphasia (d/t watershed infarct MCA, PCA); impaired repetition in that branch gives Broca's aphasia. (Book p567)

questions.q: The flowchart's Broca's aphasia arm lists which cluster?
opts: Agrammatic (telegraphic) speech, poor reading/writing, associated weakness, good comprehension
Echolalia with intact comprehension and repetition
Loud reading, writing formed with errors, no weakness
questions.exp: Broca's aphasia in the flowchart: agrammatic (telegraphic), poor reading/writing, associated sign weakness and good comprehension; motor aphasia overall is non-fluent speech: DESP (dysarthria, effortful, sparse with reduced word output, prosody lost, naming impaired). (Book p567)

questions.q: Sensory aphasia is described as fluent speech with which features?
opts: Jargon speech (pen -> hen), neologisms, logorrhoea, impaired naming (paraphasia)
Non-fluent, effortful, sparse speech with prosody lost
questions.exp: Sensory aphasia: fluent speech with jargon substitution (eg pen -> hen), neologisms (create new words), logorrhoea (increased word output) and naming impaired (paraphasia). (Book p567)

questions.q: Comprehension preserved but repetition impaired in the flowchart gives which aphasia and lesion?
opts: Conduction aphasia, lesion of the arcuate fasciculus
Anomic aphasia, lesion of the angular gyrus
questions.exp: Preserved comprehension with impaired repetition = conduction aphasia (arcuate fasciculus lesion); preserved repetition in that branch = anomic aphasia (angular gyrus lesion); impaired comprehension with preserved repetition = transcortical sensory aphasia (d/t infarct). (Book p568)

questions.q: Comprehension impaired and repetition impaired in the flowchart: which aphasia, with which associated sign?
opts: Wernicke's aphasia, with superior quadrantanopia and no weakness
questions.exp: Impaired comprehension with impaired repetition = Wernicke's aphasia (d/t infarct; reading loud, writing formed with errors, preservation poor, associated sign superior quadrantanopia, no weakness). (Book p568)

questions.q: Which statement is printed as the note beneath the flowchart?
opts: Lesion of parietal lobe: inferior quadrantanopia
Lesion of parietal lobe: superior quadrantanopia
Lesion of occipital lobe: inferior quadrantanopia
questions.exp: Note beneath the flowchart: lesion of parietal lobe -> inferior quadrantanopia (the Wernicke's arm separately lists superior quadrantanopia). (Book p568)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the dysarthria type NOT listed in the book's four types:
questions.exp: The four printed types: cortical (in Broca's aphasia), pseudo-bulbar/spastic (corticobulbar fibres abnormality), bulbar/flaccid (LMN - brain stem nuclei and below; test sounds produced from lip, tongue and oropharynx) and cerebellar (slow scanning staccato speech). (Book p568)

questions.q: A corticobulbar (UMN, cortex to anterior horn cell) abnormality produces which dysarthria per the types list?
questions.exp: Pseudo-bulbar (spastic) dysarthria = corticobulbar fibres abnormality (UMN -> cortex to anterior horn cell); bulbar (flaccid) is LMN at brain stem nuclei and below. (Book p568)

units.title: 1. Language vs Speech & the Auditory Pathway
units.sec: Language vs Speech & the Auditory Pathway
units.guide:
Language is the dominant-hemisphere concept of communication; speech is its motor output.
The perisylvian auditory-pathway diagram assigns functions to Broca's (44,45), Wernicke's (22) and the connecting fibres.
Prosody and the brainstem-to-muscle output close the first diagram.

units.title: 2. Aphasia Lesion Map & Flowchart
units.guide:
Three note lines map fibre/lesion sites to auditory agnosia, pure word deafness and pure alexia.
The lesion-site table assigns fluency, comprehension, repetition and naming to sulcal regions.
Motor (non-fluent DESP) and sensory (fluent jargon) aphasia open the comprehension/repetition flowchart.

units.title: 3. Aphasia Flowchart Continued
units.guide:
The four remaining flowchart arms are read from comprehension x repetition.
Wernicke's arm carries its associated signs and the parietal quadrantanopia note.

units.title: 4. Dysarthria
units.guide:
Four dysarthria types are listed by their anatomical level.
Corticobulbar UMN disease maps to the spastic (pseudo-bulbar) type.
